# Read in the data
lumpyore <- readxl::read_xls(
  "~/Desktop/OU_Masters/MATH-5743_Spring_2026/K25936_Downloads/K25936_Downloads/Excel/LUMPYORE.xls"
)

1.0.1 a.

The population is all bulk specimens of Chilean lumpy iron ore in a 35,325-long-ton shipload of ore.

1.0.2 b.

One possible objective of this sampling procedure could be to estimate the percentage of iron in the shipment of ore.

1.0.3 c.

# First get the number of classes
if (length(lumpyore$PCTIRON) < 25) {
  nclass <- 6
} else if (length(lumpyore$PCTIRON) >= 25 &
           length(lumpyore$PCTIRON) <= 50) {
  nclass <- 8
} else{
  nclass <- 12
}

# Then make the histogram
hist(
  lumpyore$PCTIRON,
  freq = FALSE,
  nclass = nclass,
  main = "Histogram of Lumpy Iron Ore Data",
  xlab = "Percent of Iron in Ore",
  ylab = "Relative Frequencies"
)

1.0.4 d.

# Calculate mean
mean(lumpyore$PCTIRON)
## [1] 62.96348
# Calculate stdev
sd(lumpyore$PCTIRON)
## [1] 0.6085329

1.0.5 e.

# Calculate our bounds
CI_L <- mean(lumpyore$PCTIRON) - 2 * sd(lumpyore$PCTIRON)
CI_U <- mean(lumpyore$PCTIRON) + 2 * sd(lumpyore$PCTIRON)

# Calculate the proportion of observations within our bounds
pk <- length(lumpyore$PCTIRON[lumpyore$PCTIRON > CI_L &
                                lumpyore$PCTIRON < CI_U]) / length(lumpyore$PCTIRON)

# Convert to percent
percent_pk <- pk * 100

# Print both proportion and percent
pk
## [1] 0.969697
percent_pk
## [1] 96.9697

The empirical rule states that approximately 95% of the measurements will fall within 2 standard deviations of their mean, and here 96.97% of the lumpy ore observations are within 2 standard deviations of their mean. Therefore, in a strict sense this percentage technically does not agree with the empirical rule since more of the observations are captured in the interval. However, if we are more lenient then we can say it does agree with the empirical rule because 96.97% is close to the approximation of 95%.

1.0.6 f.

# Finding the quantiles using quantile()
probs <- c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90) # vector of percentiles we want
quantile(lumpyore$PCTIRON, probs = probs) # calculates the percentiles
##     25%     50%     75%     90% 
## 62.6075 63.0100 63.3425 63.6750

These values represent how the bulk specimens of Chilean lumpy iron ore can be divided up. 25% of the bulk specimens have less than or equal to 62.6075% iron in them, 50% of the bulk specimens have less than or equal to 63.0100% iron in them, 75% of the bulk specimens have less than or equal to 63.3425% iron in them, and 90% of the bulk specimens have less than or equal to 63.6750% iron in them.

gobiants <- readxl::read_xls(

)

2.0.1 a.

# mean of ant species from all 11 sites
mean(gobiants$AntSpecies)
## [1] 12.81818
# median of ant species from all 11 sites
median(gobiants$AntSpecies)
## [1] 5
# mode of ant species from all 11 sites
DescTools::Mode(gobiants$AntSpecies)
## [1] 4 5
## attr(,"freq")
## [1] 3

The mean is 12.81 which represents the average number of ant species observed per study site (even though 0.81 species doesn’t make sense so it can be round to 13 or 12 for approximately that many species per study site).

The median is 5 which represents the middle value (number of observed species) when the column is ordered from lowest to highest. It means that 50% of the study sites have 5 species or less and the other 50% have 5 species or more.

The mode is 4 and 5 because both occur 3 times and represent the most frequent amount of observed ant species across all sites.

2.0.2 b.

The measure of central tendency I would recommend here is the median because upon looking at the data 9 sites have less than 10 observed species while two sites have 40 or more observed species. Therefore, these sites with high values inflate the mean and skew the distribution of our data. The median in this case would better represent the center of our distribution of data because it is resistant to the influence of those sites with a higher number of species and still accounts for them.

3 Question 5

# Begin writing the function that works on a vector x of quantitative data and uses k standard deviations
mydescr <- function(x, k) {
  # first it needs to generate 1x2 plots using layout or par(mfrow)
  par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) # allows for plotting in a 1x2 window
  
  # use if else statements to define number of classes based on sample size of vector
  if (length(x) < 25) {
    nclass <- 6
  } else if (length(x) >= 25 & length(x) <= 50) {
    nclass <- 8
  } else{
    nclass <- 12
  }
  
  # generates histogram of vector x with specified number of classes
  hist <- hist(
    x,
    nclass = nclass,
    main = "Histogram of x",
    xlab = "x",
    ylab = "Frequency"
  )
  
  # generates notched boxplot of vector x with a range of 3 to extend the whiskers out to 3 * the upper and lower quartiles for outlier detection
  box <-  boxplot(x, notch = TRUE, range = 3)
  
  par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) # reset plotting window to 1x1
  
  # second we need a named list returning the IQR, mean, stdev, vector of possible outliers (defined by z), vector of outliers (defined by z), vector of outliers define by the box plot and the proportion pk of data within k stdev from the mean
  
  IQR <- IQR(x) # IQR of x
  xbar <- mean(x) # mean of x
  stdev <- sd(x) # stdev of x
  z_scores <- (x - xbar) / stdev # z-scores for x
  v_possible <- x[abs(z_scores) >= 2 &
                    abs(z_scores) <= 3] # possible outliers based on the rule of thumb from MS page 59
  v_outliers_z <- x[abs(z_scores) > 3] # outliers defined by z
  v_boxplot_out <- box$out # outliers defined from the boxplot where the values extend 3 * the upper and lower quartiles
  CI_L <- xbar - k * stdev # lower bound for values within k*stdev
  CI_U <- xbar + k * stdev # upper bound for values within
  pk <- length(x[x > CI_L &
                   x < CI_U]) / (length(x)) # proportion of values within +/- k*stdev
  pChebk <- 1 - (1 / (k^2)) # minimal quantity defined by Chebyshev
  stndpk <- (pk - pChebk) / (sqrt((pk * (1 - pk) / length(x)))) # standardized difference between pk and pChebk
  
  # make named list with all calculations
  out <- list(
    IQR = IQR,
    mean = xbar,
    stdev = stdev,
    possible_out = v_possible,
    z_out = v_outliers_z,
    box_out = v_boxplot_out,
    pk = pk,
    stndpk = stndpk,
    z = z_scores
  )
  
  return(out) # returns named list
  
}
# Read in data
fatal <- readxl::read_xls(
  "~/Desktop/OU_Masters/MATH-5743_Spring_2026/K25936_Downloads/K25936_Downloads/Excel/FATAL.XLS"
)

# Evaluate function for fatal data set and k = 2
mydescr(fatal$Fatalities, k = 2)
